nodes.name: Shared context is most useful when it reaches the places…
nodes.text: Shared context is most useful when it reaches the places your product actually runs. A marketing site wants published pages. A support widget wants the current help articles. A build script wants the latest translation files. A backend service wants to look something up in the team’s Memory.

nodes.name: On 20 November 2026 we published client SDKs that make…
nodes.text: On 20 November 2026 we published client SDKs that make those reads straightforward, as early access releases at version 0.1.0. They are open source under the MIT license in [github.com/doubco/nulldull-sdks](https://github.com/doubco/nulldull-sdks).

nodes.name: There are six SDKs: `@nulldull/sdk` for Node.js and…
nodes.text: There are six SDKs: `@nulldull/sdk` for Node.js and TypeScript, `@nulldull/react` for React, `nulldull` for Python, a Go module at `github.com/doubco/nulldull-sdks/go`, `NullDull` for Swift through Swift Package Manager, and `com.nulldull:nulldull-sdk` for Kotlin and Android.

nodes.name: All six follow one specification and share one conformance…
nodes.text: All six follow one specification and share one conformance suite, so the same call behaves the same way in each language. Errors carry the API’s code, detail and request ID. Reads are retried at most twice, and only after a rate limit or a temporary server error.

nodes.name: The SDKs read published Grid content, Memory and Locale…
nodes.text: The SDKs read published Grid content, Memory and Locale exports. They never write. Changing content goes through the app, the agent connection or the HTTP API, where reviews, version checks and receipts apply.

nodes.name: This is a deliberate split. Reading published or shared…
nodes.text: This is a deliberate split. Reading published or shared content is something many parts of a product need, often from places where a person isn’t present to approve anything. Writing shared content is a decision that benefits from review and attribution, so it stays with the interfaces built for that. Keeping the SDKs read-only makes them simple to reason about. A key embedded in a mobile app can only ever read what was explicitly published. A key on a server can only read what the member who created it can read, and only within the access it was given.

nodes.name: The SDKs use workspace API keys, which owners and admins…
nodes.text: The SDKs use workspace API keys, which owners and admins create under Workspace settings → API keys. A **public** key reads only published Grid content and is safe to ship in browser and mobile apps. A **private** key is shown once, belongs on a server, and can additionally read Memory or export Locale catalogs as the member who created it, limited to that member’s current access.

nodes.name: Memory and Locale calls need the workspace ID, because a…
nodes.text: Memory and Locale calls need the workspace ID, because a key cannot look up its own workspace. The React SDK refuses a private key in a browser, which turns a common mistake into an error instead of a leak.

nodes.name: Alongside the SDKs, `@nulldull/grid-core` and…
nodes.text: Alongside the SDKs, `@nulldull/grid-core` and `@nulldull/grid-react` are published on npm at 0.1.0 as early access packages. The core package holds the Grid document types, validation and responsive geometry; the React package renders published pages with every built-in node, layout and font feature.

nodes.name: Native Grid renderers for Swift and Kotlin also exist as…
nodes.text: Native Grid renderers for Swift and Kotlin also exist as source in our repository. They are alpha packages and not yet published to Swift Package Manager or Maven Central; we will announce them on What’s new? when they are.
